Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Mateo sits stiffly in the chair, his calloused welder's hands resting on his knees, palms down, as if to hold himself in place. At seventy, his body is a testament to a life of hard, physical work, but his eyes are far older, carrying the weight of something that happened nearly fifty years ago in a country he has not seen since. The story has lived inside him, mostly in silence. It was in a small, windowless room where his life fractured. He had been a university student, full of political fervour and loud opinions. He came to believe this was his fatal error; the event, he remains certain, happened because of the way he acted, because he had been too bold. They took him in the night. The memory isn't a neat narrative he can recount. When he has tried, perhaps for his late wife, Elena, the words would tangle and choke him. He would start to explain the feeling of the rough concrete floor against his cheek, the smell of stale sweat and fear, and then the thread would vanish, leaving him adrift in a sea of raw sensation he could not articulate.

What he remembers most clearly are the moments of utter paralysis. He recalls one of his captors explaining, with chilling calm, all the things that were about to happen to him, and the absolute certainty that there was no way out. This feeling of being trapped, of having no options, is the ghost that haunts his waking life. It can find him anywhere. Last month, at the fabrication shop, his foreman boxed him into a corner on a tight deadline for a complex pipe fitting. As the foreman stood over him, listing the impossible demands, the workshop air suddenly grew thin and heavy, the scent of ozone from the welding torch turning metallic and sharp, like blood. Mateo felt the old, familiar helplessness wash over him. He became overly compliant, nodding, agreeing to everything, his voice a strained whisper. It was the only way he knew to survive a threat: make himself small, agreeable, invisible. He saw the foreman's surprise, but the internal storm of rage and shame was so consuming he could barely register it. He felt an intense, burning anger at the man, but even more so at himself. He will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened all those years ago, for not fighting back in that room, and every time he fawns and complies now, it feels like the same failure, repeated.

The memories, when they break through the dam of suppression he has spent a lifetime building, are not memories at all. They are present-tense ambushes. A car backfiring on his street is not a similar sound; it is the sound of the pistol being cocked beside his ear, the cold click of the hammer echoing in the silent room. In that instant, he is no longer a 70-year-old widower in his quiet Chicago neighbourhood; he is twenty years old and on the floor, convinced his life is over. The past collapses into the present with a terrifying, visceral force. To cope, he learned to float away. When the images start to flicker-a face contorted in a sneer, the glint of a tool-he detaches, watching the scene as if it's a poorly made film happening to a stranger. It's a desperate attempt to create distance, but the rage always finds him. The rage is pure and clean, a searing fury at his torturers, but it quickly curdles into self-blame.

For decades, Elena was his anchor. Her presence was a buffer, a reason to keep the past locked away. Since her death last year, the silence in their small house has become cavernous, and the memories fill the void. He feels exposed, believing you can never know who will harm you, scanning the faces of neighbours with a suspicion that feels both exhausting and necessary. The old strategies are failing. Trying hard not to think about it is like trying to hold back the tide. He is afraid of his own anger, afraid of the moments he loses the thread of his own life story, afraid that one day, the memory will ambush him and he won't come back. It was after a particularly bad week, where he found himself apologising to a dismissive clerk at the grocery store with the same desperate energy he once used to plead for his life, that he finally made the call. He came to therapy not with a clear goal, but with the exhausted plea of a man who has been fighting the same war for fifty years and can no longer bear to fight it alone.
